dimethicone.text: Dimethicone is used in primers, moisturizers and hair serums to leave a smooth, silky film that visibly softens the look of fine lines and pores and adds shine to hair. The smoothing is visible on application; trials cover medical skin-protectant uses rather than long-term appearance outcomes.

shea-butter.text: Shea butter is used as a rich moisturizer for dry skin, lips and hair ends, so skin looks softer and less flaky. It is promoted on the basis of traditional use and lab composition data; trials of shea butter alone for appearance are not found.

sodium-pca.text: Sodium PCA is a humectant in moisturizers and toners, used to keep skin hydrated so it looks plumper and less dry. It occurs naturally in skin's moisturizing factor; safety is reviewed, but trials of the ingredient alone for appearance were not found.

sodium-lactate.text: Sodium lactate appears in moisturizers and cleansers as a humectant and pH adjuster, used to help skin hold water and feel softer. It is the salt of lactic acid, a familiar exfoliating acid, though its own appearance effects are less documented than its medical roles.

trehalose.text: Trehalose is added to some moisturizers and serums as a water-binding, protective sugar, and is discussed in anti-aging circles for its link to autophagy. Autophagy findings come from lab and animal research; appearance trials on skin are not found.

chain: Polymer binds large amounts of water
polyglutamic-acid.text: Polyglutamic acid is promoted in serums and essences as a humectant said to hold more water than hyaluronic acid, giving a plump, dewy look. Its established clinical use is as a drug carrier; appearance claims rest mainly on lab comparisons and brand testing.

propanediol.text: Propanediol is a base ingredient in serums and moisturizers, used to hydrate, improve texture and help other actives dissolve and spread. It is chosen as a plant-derived alternative to propylene glycol; its role is supporting formulations rather than a studied appearance treatment.

ectoin.text: Ectoin is used in soothing and barrier-support skincare, promoted to reduce redness and protect against UV and pollution stress for calmer, more even-looking skin. Lab data on UV stress exist; trials on appearance in healthy skin are not found.

beta-glucan.text: Oat and yeast beta-glucan is used in creams and serums for soothing and hydration, so skin looks calmer and less dry. It is well studied as dietary fibre and an immune trigger; use as a topical appearance treatment is largely untested.

allantoin.text: Allantoin is a common drugstore additive in moisturizers, lip balms and after-shave products, used to soften rough skin and calm irritation. It also appears in scar and wound combination products; allantoin tested on its own for appearance is rare.

phytosphingosine.text: Phytosphingosine is added to barrier-repair and blemish-prone skincare as a precursor to the skin's own ceramides, with the aim of reducing dryness and breakouts. Cosmetic trials of it were not found in the sources reviewed.

cholesterol.text: Cholesterol is included in ceramide-based moisturizers because it makes up roughly a third of the skin's barrier lipid mix, helping restore a dry or damaged barrier. It is used as part of lipid blends; appearance trials on its own were not found.

squalene.text: Squalane and squalene are used as light, non-greasy emollients in moisturizers and facial oils to soften skin and add glow. Squalene is a natural component of skin sebum; trials for appearance outcomes are not found.

natto-gum.text: Natto gum is used in Japanese and Korean face packs and essences as a humectant that holds water on the skin, associated with poly-gamma-glutamic acid. Its use is documented in patents and product descriptions rather than human trials.

lauric-acid.text: Lauric acid, abundant in coconut oil, is mostly a soap and cleanser raw material, and some users apply it with the idea of reducing acne bacteria for clearer skin. Antibacterial data come from lab studies; skin appearance trials are not found.

panthenol.text: Panthenol is a staple of moisturizers, hair products and wound creams, used to hydrate skin, calm irritation and leave hair smoother. Human data mainly cover skin hydration and wound healing.

jojoba-oil.text: Jojoba oil is used as a facial moisturizer and carrier oil because its wax esters resemble skin's own sebum, and is popular for softening skin and hair. It is widely used and valued by users; controlled trials on appearance are limited.

tamanu-oil.text: Tamanu oil is promoted in natural-skincare circles for fading scars and acne marks and calming breakouts, drawing on traditional Pacific use for wounds and burns. Support comes from lab cell data and tradition; human trials are not found.

meadowfoam-seed-oil.text: Meadowfoam seed oil is used in creams, lip products and hair care as a light, very stable emollient that softens skin and adds shine. Its appeal is largely formulation stability; published human skin-benefit trials are not found.

sea-buckthorn-oil.text: Sea buckthorn oil is used in creams and supplements for its orange carotenoid-rich profile, promoted for moisturizing, glow and skin repair. Small human trials exist, but skin-specific appearance evidence is limited.

chain: Support for skin barrier and inflammation
evening-primrose-oil.text: Evening primrose oil is taken as a supplement or applied topically for dry, eczema-prone or hormonally breakout-prone skin. Reviews of its use for eczema find insufficient evidence, and appearance trials in healthy skin are not found.

macadamia-oil.text: Macadamia oil is used in moisturizers, body oils and hair products as a rich emollient, with interest in its palmitoleic acid, which is also found in skin sebum. Composition research exists; clear human skin-appearance trials are not found.

grapeseed-oil.text: Grapeseed oil is used as a lightweight facial and massage oil, often chosen by people with oily or breakout-prone skin who want moisture without heaviness. Its linoleic acid content is documented; published trials on skin appearance are not found.

black-rice-extract.text: Black rice extract is promoted in anti-aging and brightening skincare for its anthocyanin pigments, which act as antioxidants. Lab and animal work is plentiful; human skin evidence was not found.

propolis.text: Propolis is a K-beauty staple in ampoules and creams, used for calming breakouts, soothing skin and giving a glowy finish. Antimicrobial data come from lab studies; skin-specific human evidence is limited.

honey-topical.text: Honey is used in DIY masks and skincare as a humectant for soft, hydrated skin, and some users apply it for brightening and blemishes. It has real wound-care data; controlled evidence for skin brightening is not yet available.

bee-venom-topical.text: Topical bee venom is marketed in Korean skincare as a natural alternative to botulinum toxin, with brands claiming it tightens skin and smooths expression lines. Wrinkle trials of the topical product were not found.

chain: Yeast ferment of vitamins and amino acids
galactomyces-ferment-filtrate.text: Galactomyces ferment filtrate, sold in Japanese and Korean essences such as Pitera, is used for brightening, hydration and a smoother glow. Evidence includes cell-lab data and product studies; isolated human trials are few.

bifida-ferment-lysate.text: Bifida ferment lysate is used in repair and barrier serums as a probiotic-derived active, promoted for soothing, resilience and a more youthful look. Lab barrier data exist; human trials are limited to combination products.

lactobacillus-ferment.text: Lactobacillus ferment appears in K-beauty and probiotic skincare creams, used for barrier support and calming sensitive or reddened skin. Skin-specific human evidence is limited.
